- [ ] 1.4 Implement the JSON report as a single document containing every finding, valid and
      well-formed even when the finding set is empty.
- [ ] 1.5 Implement the severity-to-exit-status mapping: `0` when no error, `2` when any error, and
      the runtime-failure status for a lint failure such as an unreadable lockfile.
- [ ] 1.6 Implement strict mode promoting warnings to errors for exit purposes only.

## 2. Local checks

- [ ] 2.1 Implement the manifest check, reporting a load or validation failure as a single finding and
      suppressing the checks that depend on it.
- [ ] 2.2 Implement the declared-but-not-installed check against the lockfile.
- [ ] 2.3 Implement the stale-lockfile-entry check for assets no longer declared or no longer
      targeting a harness.
- [ ] 2.4 Implement the missing-lockfile case as an informational "nothing installed yet" rather than
      an error.
- [ ] 2.5 Implement content integrity: recompute every installed file's digest and compare against the
      recorded value, reporting modified files individually.
- [ ] 2.6 Implement missing-file and absent-destination detection, collapsing a wholly missing
      destination into one finding.
- [ ] 2.7 Implement extraneous-file detection for files present under a managed destination that the
      installation record does not list.
- [ ] 2.8 Implement the unmanaged-conflict check for a declared asset whose destination exists but is
      unrecorded.

## 3. Update detection

- [ ] 3.1 Implement moved-mutable-ref detection comparing a re-resolved branch or default-branch ref
      against the recorded commit.
- [ ] 3.2 Implement the vanished-ref case as a finding distinct from an available update.
- [ ] 3.3 Implement superseded-tag detection: list tags, compare by semantic version, report only the
      highest newer one, ignore non-version tags, and never offer a pre-release over a stable install.
- [ ] 3.4 Implement the rule that a commit-pinned asset is never reported as outdated and triggers no
      remote lookup.
- [ ] 3.5 Implement the mutable-ref advisory warning suggesting a pin.
- [ ] 3.6 Implement local source change detection by re-reading `.harnaas` and comparing digests, and
      distinguish a deleted local source from a change.
- [ ] 3.7 Implement the resolution cache with a bounded freshness window, forced refresh, and
      discard-on-corruption.
- [ ] 3.8 Implement graceful degradation: mark affected assets unchecked, report a host failure once
      rather than per asset, distinguish an authorization failure, and keep the exit status decided by
      the checks that ran.

## 4. Command wiring

- [ ] 4.1 Add `lint.go` with the command constructor and its offline, strict, refresh and JSON flags.
- [ ] 4.2 Wire the local checks and update detection into a single pass, reusing the resolution and
      transport built for install.
- [ ] 4.3 Enforce the read-only guarantee: no code path in the lint flow writes outside the user cache
      directory.
- [ ] 4.4 Implement offline mode skipping every network check while still running local source change
      detection, and note the skip in the report.

## 5. Tests

- [ ] 5.1 Add a test asserting that a lint run over a project with many findings leaves every project
      and harness file byte-for-byte unchanged.
- [ ] 5.2 Add table-driven tests for each local check over temporary projects: drift, missing file,
      absent destination, extraneous file, unmanaged conflict, not installed, stale entry.
- [ ] 5.3 Add a test asserting an invalid manifest yields exactly one finding with no cascade.
- [ ] 5.4 Add exit-status tests: clean, warnings only, errors present, strict mode, and a lint failure
      distinguished from findings.
- [ ] 5.5 Add update-detection tests against a local remote covering a moved branch, a vanished ref, a
      newer stable tag, several newer tags, a pre-release, non-version tags, and a commit pin.
- [ ] 5.6 Add local source change tests covering an edited source, a deleted source, and running under
      offline mode.
- [ ] 5.7 Add cache tests for reuse within the window, refresh past it, forced refresh, and
      discard-on-corruption.
- [ ] 5.8 Add degradation tests asserting an unreachable host does not fail the run, is reported once
      per host, and that unchecked counts appear in the summary.
- [ ] 5.9 Add report tests asserting deterministic ordering and that the JSON document is valid with an
      empty finding set.

## 6. Verification

- [ ] 6.1 Run `mise run fmt`, then `mise run lint`, then `mise run test`, re-running lint after any
      formatting change.
- [ ] 6.2 In a scratch project, install assets, edit one installed file, delete another, and confirm
      lint reports both with the correct paths, severities and remedies.
- [ ] 6.3 Confirm the reported remedy command actually resolves the finding when run.
- [ ] 6.4 Confirm exit status is `2` with errors present, `0` with only warnings, and `0` in strict
      mode only when there are no findings at all.
- [ ] 6.5 Confirm lint completes with local findings intact while the network is unavailable, and that
      the summary reports the unchecked assets.
- [ ] 6.6 Add `harnaas lint` to the project's own CI workflow as a gate.

Done. Three OpenSpec change proposals authored and validated.

## What was created

```
openspec/changes/
├── add-harnaas-foundation/   3 deltas · 25 requirements · 46 tasks
│   └── specs/{cli-foundation, harnaas-manifest, init-command}/
├── add-harnaas-install/      4 deltas · 39 requirements · 54 tasks
│   └── specs/{source-resolution, harness-targets, install-command, install-lockfile}/
└── add-harnaas-lint/         2 deltas · 15 requirements · 41 tasks
    └── specs/{lint-command, update-detection}/
```

Each has `proposal.md`, `design.md`, `tasks.md`, and its delta specs. `openspec validate --changes --strict` passes 3/3; all three report `isPlanningComplete: true`.

## Key design calls

**Ownership is the lockfile, not an in-file marker.** The entire.io CLI marks files it scaffolds, but it *generates* that content. harnaas *copies* content verbatim — injecting a marker would break byte-equality with upstream and defeat the very drift detection it enables. So a path recorded in `harnaas.lock.json` is managed; a path absent from it is the user's and is never overwritten, even with `--force`. The one exception is the generated `CLAUDE.md` rules block, which harnaas authors itself.

**Archive fetch, Git ref resolution.** Refs resolve over the Git protocol (no API rate limit, uses existing credential helpers); bytes move over HTTPS as one repository archive per commit. Per-file REST requests would exhaust an unauthenticated rate limit on a single CI install.

**Decoding strictness follows who writes the file.** `harnaas.json` is committed and hand-edited → rejects unknown fields. `harnaas.lock.json` is machine-rewritten → ignores them, so a newer binary can't brick an older one. This is entire's rule, and it lands the two files on opposite sides.

**`lint` never repairs, and exit 2 means findings.** No `--fix`: every repair is something `install` already does, and duplicating overwrite/convergence logic in two commands means two implementations that must agree forever. Exit 2 is the one documented deviation from entire's contract (which uses `1` for everything) — without it, CI can't tell "lint crashed" from "your harness drifted".

Two corrections to my initial reading, caught by the architecture exploration: entire declares **zero** root persistent flags (`--json` is per-command, deliberately), and the project root travels in `context.Context` rather than via a `-C` flag. Both are now specified that way.

I also filled in `openspec/config.yaml`'s `context:` block with the stack and conventions, so later artifacts inherit them without re-deriving.

**Nothing was implemented** — no `go.mod`, no source. The propose workflow authorizes planning only; implementation is a separate `/opsx:apply` pass.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline — challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill — that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up — capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

# CONTEXT.md Format

## Structure

```md
# {Context Name}

{One or two sentence description of what this context is and why it exists.}

## Language

**Order**:
{A one or two sentence description of the term}
_Avoid_: Purchase, transaction

**Invoice**:
A request for payment sent to a customer after delivery.
_Avoid_: Bill, payment request

**Customer**:
A person or organization that places orders.
_Avoid_: Client, buyer, account
```

## Rules

- **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.
- **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. Before adding a term, ask: is this a concept unique to this context, or a general programming concept? Only the former belongs.
- **Group terms under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge. If all terms belong to a single cohesive area, a flat list is fine.

## Single vs multi-context repos

**Single context (most repos):** One `CONTEXT.md` at the repo root.

**Multiple contexts:** A `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the repo root lists the contexts, where they live, and how they relate to each other:

```md
# Context Map

## Contexts

- [Ordering](./src/ordering/CONTEXT.md) — receives and tracks customer orders
- [Billing](./src/billing/CONTEXT.md) — generates invoices and processes payments
- [Fulfillment](./src/fulfillment/CONTEXT.md) — manages warehouse picking and shipping

## Relationships

- **Ordering → Fulfillment**: Ordering emits `OrderPlaced` events; Fulfillment consumes them to start picking
- **Fulfillment → Billing**: Fulfillment emits `ShipmentDispatched` events; Billing consumes them to generate invoices
- **Ordering ↔ Billing**: Shared types for `CustomerId` and `Money`
```

The skill infers which structure applies:

- If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, read it to find contexts
- If only a root `CONTEXT.md` exists, single context
- If neither exists, create a root `CONTEXT.md` lazily when the first term is resolved

When multiple contexts exist, infer which one the current topic relates to. If unclear, ask.
========= ADR =========
# ADR Format

ADRs live in `docs/adr/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc.

Create the `docs/adr/` directory lazily — only when the first ADR is needed.

## Template

```md
# {Short title of the decision}

{1-3 sentences: what's the context, what did we decide, and why.}
```

That's it. An ADR can be a single paragraph. The value is in recording *that* a decision was made and *why* — not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most ADRs won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded by ADR-NNNN`) — useful when decisions are revisited
- **Considered Options** — only when the rejected alternatives are worth remembering
- **Consequences** — only when non-obvious downstream effects need to be called out

## Numbering

Scan `docs/adr/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to offer an ADR

All three of these must be true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will look at the code and wonder "why on earth did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If a decision is easy to reverse, skip it — you'll just reverse it. If it's not surprising, nobody will wonder why. If there was no real alternative, there's nothing to record beyond "we did the obvious thing."

### What qualifies

- **Architectural shape.** "We're using a monorepo." "The write model is event-sourced, the read model is projected into Postgres."
- **Integration patterns between contexts.** "Ordering and Billing communicate via domain events, not synchronous HTTP."
- **Technology choices that carry lock-in.** Database, message bus, auth provider, deployment target. Not every library — just the ones that would take a quarter to swap out.
- **Boundary and scope decisions.** "Customer data is owned by the Customer context; other contexts reference it by ID only." The explicit no-s are as valuable as the yes-s.
- **Deliberate deviations from the obvious path.** "We're using manual SQL instead of an ORM because X." Anything where a reasonable reader would assume the opposite. These stop the next engineer from "fixing" something that was deliberate.
- **Constraints not visible in the code.** "We can't use AWS because of compliance requirements." "Response times must be under 200ms because of the partner API contract."
- **Rejected alternatives when the rejection is non-obvious.** If you considered GraphQL and picked REST for subtle reasons, record it — otherwise someone will suggest GraphQL again in six months.

# Round 1

I wrote ~79 requirements' worth of decisions into those specs, many of which I made unilaterally. This round is the root of the tree — five questions that everything downstream hangs off. Two facts are being looked up in the background (Claude Code's real extension surfaces; cross-harness vocabulary), so the questions that depend on those are held for round 2.

---

❓ **Q1** — **Who is this for?**: The whole design leans one way or the other depending on the answer, and I never asked. Two coherent products live inside "harnaas":

**(a) Team standardization.** `harnaas.json` and `harnaas.lock.json` are committed. The point is that everyone on the repo gets the same skills and rules, and CI can enforce it. Project scope is the main path; user scope is a niche escape hatch.

**(b) Personal portability.** You declare your preferred setup once and reproduce it on every machine you work on. User scope is the main path; the "project" is really just where your declaration happens to live. CI enforcement is meaningless.

These pull apart hard. In (a), a committed lockfile is essential and a user-scoped entry in it is noise. In (b), the committed lockfile records paths that only exist on one machine, and my "scope-relative paths so it's machine-independent" requirement is solving a problem you don't have.

➡️ **(a) Team standardization as primary**, personal portability supported but secondary. It's what your `install`-scope answer already implied, and it's the version where `lint` earns its place. If you actually want (b), I should reopen the lockfile design — it's specified for a use case it might not have.

---

❓ **Q2** — **What do we call the thing being installed?**: I used **asset** throughout ("harness assets"), covering skills, rules, commands and subagents. I picked it in about four seconds and then wrote it into nine spec files.

Candidates: `asset` (neutral, covers plain files, slightly content-marketing), `artifact` (collides with build artifacts and with the lockfile's own "recorded artifact" sense), `extension` (implies executable behaviour; three of the four types are just markdown), `resource` (too vague to be worth a word), `capability` (already load-bearing in OpenSpec — it's the unit specs are organized by, so reusing it here would be actively confusing), `component`, `module`.

Note the one real collision to avoid: **plugin**. Claude Code has its own plugin system with marketplaces, and entire.io has a separate plugin concept. Whatever we pick must not be that word.

### Plugin on-disk structure

Manifest **must** be at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`; components **must** be at plugin root, not inside `.claude-plugin/`. Canonical layout, straight from the official `plugin-structure` skill:

```
plugin-name/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json    # required
├── commands/*.md
├── agents/*.md
├── skills/<name>/SKILL.md
├── hooks/hooks.json
├── .mcp.json
└── scripts/
```

Auto-discovery scans those default dirs. `plugin.json` may add `commands` / `agents` / `hooks` / `mcpServers` / `skills` path overrides which **supplement rather than replace** the defaults; they must be relative and start with `./`. Name must match `/^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/`. `version` defaults to `"0.1.0"`.

Two real, contrasting manifests:

`mattpocock-skills` uses an **explicit `skills` array** of 25 paths (skills nested two levels deep under `skills/engineering/` and `skills/productivity/`, which auto-discovery would not find):
```json

  "author": {"name":"Matt Pocock","url":"https://www.aihero.dev"},
  "homepage": "...", "repository": "...", "license": "MIT", "keywords": [...],
  "skills": ["./skills/engineering/ask-matt", "./skills/engineering/tdd", ...] }
```

`figma` relies on auto-discovery plus a root `.mcp.json`, and ships parallel `.cursor-plugin/` and `gemini-extension.json` for other hosts.

`superpowers` demonstrates hooks — `hooks/hooks.json`:
```json
{ "hooks": { "SessionStart": [ { "matcher": "startup|clear|compact",
  "hooks": [ { "type":"command",
    "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/run-hook.cmd\" session-start",
    "shell":"bash", "async": false } ] } ] } }
```
Note `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` — mandatory for portability, since the install path is version-scoped and unpredictable. Note also that `superpowers` ships a `.cmd` wrapper specifically for Windows.

Both `plugin.json` files are the 3-field minimum (`name`, `description`, `version: "1.0.0"`). Neither plugin has skills, agents, hooks, or MCP — commands only. The commands use bare frontmatter (`description` only) and delegate to skill files by path:

## 3. Memory / rules loading

### `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`

Both are hardcoded. Binary string, from the Codex config importer explaining why a Codex setting has no equivalent:

> `Claude Code hardcodes CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md discovery.`

Files loaded, by scope:
- **Managed:** `<managedDir>/.claude/rules/` (type `Managed`, cannot be excluded)
- **User:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `~/.claude/rules/**.md`
- **Project:** `./CLAUDE.md`, `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `./.claude/rules/**.md` — plus a **walk up every ancestor directory** to the filesystem root, and a descent into nested directories (nested `CLAUDE.md` loads when you work under that directory, load reason `nested_traversal`)
- **Local:** `./CLAUDE.local.md`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`

Confirmed by the binary's own `/init` guidance:
> LOCAL files: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and `CLAUDE.local.md` (project root and ancestor dirs). Checked-in files: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md` in the project, including nested directories.

Also present: an `InstructionsLoaded` hook event carrying `file_path`, `memory_type`, `load_reason`, `globs`, `trigger_file_path`, `parent_file_path` — a clean way to verify your installer's rules actually loaded.

Kill switch: env var `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_MDS` disables the whole memory system. Extra roots: `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD`.

### `@path` import syntax — works, documented, but do not use it here

Verified. Internally called `@include`. Evidence:
- Error string: ``Skipping non-text file in @include: ${t}`` with an extension allowlist
- Recursion with a depth counter: `$be(f, t, r, n, o+1, e)`
- Consent gate for imports that escape the repo: `"Allow external CLAUDE.md file imports?"` and `"This project's CLAUDE.md imports files outside the current working directory. Never allow this for third-party repositories."`
- State flag `hasClaudeMdExternalIncludes`; a fallback path logs ``fell back to @path ref``
- The bundled `/init` skill instructs Claude to write a one-line stub `@~/.claude/<project-name>-instructions.md` for external worktrees — with the explicit warning: *"Never put this import in the project CLAUDE.md — that would check a personal reference into the team-shared file."*

Real usage on this machine: `C:\Users\brasp\Documents\GitHub\website\CLAUDE.md` is exactly one line, `@AGENTS.md`. That is the canonical "make CLAUDE.md defer to AGENTS.md" idiom.

### Verdict on your specified mechanism

`.claude/rules/` — **correct, use it.** It is the officially blessed pattern. The bundled `/init` skill says so:

> For projects with multiple concerns, suggest organizing instructions into `.claude/rules/` as separate focused files (e.g., `code-style.md`, `testing.md`, `security.md`). These are loaded automatically alongside CLAUDE.md and can be scoped to specific file paths using `paths` frontmatter.

The managed import block in `CLAUDE.md` — **delete it from your spec.** Three reasons: (a) rules already load automatically, so the block is redundant; (b) `@`-importing a file that is also auto-loaded risks double-injection; (c) editing a team-shared `CLAUDE.md` is exactly the kind of self-modification the binary's own safety prompt flags — it lists `.claude/rules/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/settings*.json`, `.claude/hooks/`, `.claude/commands/`, `.claude/agents/`, `.claude/skills/` as "config surfaces" subject to a Self-Modification review gate. Writing *files into* `.claude/rules/` is a clean additive install; *rewriting* the user's `CLAUDE.md` is not.

There is also a first-class opt-out you should respect rather than reinvent: settings key for excluding memory files, described as
> "Glob patterns or absolute paths of CLAUDE.md files to exclude from loading… Only applies to User, Project, and Local memory types (Managed/policy files cannot be excluded). Examples: `/home/user/monorepo/CLAUDE.md`, `**/code/CLAUDE.md`, `**/some-dir/.claude/rules/**`"

Note the third example is literally a `.claude/rules/**` exclusion — further confirmation the directory is a normal, expected memory source.

---

## 4. Precedence and scopes

Internal source identifiers, verified: `policySettings`, `flagSettings`, `userSettings`, `projectSettings`, `localSettings`. Ordered arrays in the binary (`"policySettings","projectSettings","localSettings"`, `"localSettings","projectSettings","userSettings"`, etc.) and this diagnostic string confirm the direction:

> `posture (projectSettings overrides userSettings in the merged read). Remove it from the repo settings; operator posture belongs in the user-level settings.json`

Effective precedence, lowest → highest: **user → project → local → policy/managed** (with `flagSettings` from CLI flags alongside policy at the top).

Locations on **Windows**:

| Scope | Path | Verified |
|---|---|---|
| Enterprise / managed | `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json`, plus a `managed-settings.d\*.json` drop-in dir | binary |
| Enterprise / policy | HKLM registry key `SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode` (and HKCU in the WSL chain) | binary |
| User | `C:\Users\brasp\.claude\settings.json` | on disk |
| Project | `<repo>\.claude\settings.json` (committed) | on disk (harnaas) |
| Local | `<repo>\.claude\settings.local.json` (gitignored) | binary |

Binary string on the enterprise sources:
> `…in either admin-only Windows source — the HKLM SOFTWARE/Policies/ClaudeCode registry key or C:/Program Files/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json — WSL reads managed settings from the full Windows policy chain (HKLM, C:/Program Files/ClaudeCode via DrvFs, HKCU) in addition to /etc/claude-code.`

(POSIX equivalents also present: `/etc/claude-code/`, `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode`.)

The scope split is also the documented default for installers — from the bundled `/init` skill:
> `Target file: default based on the Phase 1 CLAUDE.md choice — project → .claude/settings.json (team-shared, committed); personal → .claude/settings.local.json.`

Two more precedence facts relevant to a CLI:
- **Memory loading is gated on settings scopes.** `.claude/rules/` only loads if `projectSettings` is an enabled source (`kg("projectSettings")`); `~/.claude/rules/` requires `userSettings`. Enterprise policy can therefore switch your rules off wholesale.
- **A malformed settings file fails silently and catastrophically:** `"A broken settings.json silently disables ALL settings from that file"`. Any writer must validate before it writes.

---

**Verified on disk / in the shipped binary:** everything above with a quoted code fragment, string, or file path — the rules loader and its four scopes, the `paths` → `globs` frontmatter parse and the `conditionalRule` partition, `~/.claude/rules` and the managed rules dir, `@include` recursion and the external-import consent prompt, all plugin/marketplace manifests and cache layout, the settings source identifiers and Windows enterprise paths, the `cli` repo marketplace contents and its two registration defects, `.claude/hooks` being permission-registration only.

**Not found, contrary to a plausible assumption:** there is no `.claude/rules/` directory anywhere under `C:\Users\brasp\Documents\GitHub\`. The feature is supported but currently unused on this machine — so nothing here demonstrates it working end to end; the evidence is the loader code, not a live example.

---

## Recommendation

Install **raw files**, not a plugin, for rules. Rules have no plugin equivalent — `plugin.json` has no `rules` key and no plugin in the official marketplace ships one. `.claude/rules/*.md` is the only route, it is auto-loaded, it needs no manifest, and it is trivially uninstallable.

Concretely:
- Write rule files to `.claude/rules/<your-cli>-<topic>.md`. Namespace the filenames so uninstall is a glob and you never collide with a user's own rules.
- **Do not touch `CLAUDE.md`.**
- Use `paths:` frontmatter only for genuinely file-scoped rules; omit it for always-on guidance.
- If you also ship commands/agents/skills, reconsider: those *do* have a plugin equivalent, and the plugin route gives you versioning, `enabledPlugins` toggling, clean uninstall, and updates. A checked-in `directory`-source marketplace at `.claude/plugins/` (the `entire-dev-tools` pattern, minus its two path bugs) is the lowest-friction version of that.
- If you must write hooks, you must edit `settings.json` — dropping files in `.claude/hooks/` will not work. Validate the JSON before writing, and prefer `settings.local.json` unless the hook is genuinely team-shared.</result>

input.content:
# harnaas

A CLI that manages a project's AI-harness configuration as a declared, versioned dependency. A team
states which assets it wants in a manifest; `harnaas install` fetches them and places them where each
harness expects; `harnaas lint` verifies that what is installed still matches what was declared.

## Language

### The things being managed

**Harness**:
An AI coding tool that reads its configuration from files in a project or a user home — Claude Code,
Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI.
_Avoid_: agent, editor, client, host, IDE

**Asset**:
A single unit of harness configuration that harnaas installs — one skill, rule, instruction, command
or persona.
_Avoid_: artifact, resource, plugin, extension, capability

### Asset types

**Skill**:
An asset the harness loads on its own initiative when its description matches the task at hand.
_Avoid_: capability

**Rule**:
Always-on guidance installed as its own file, which the harness discovers and loads automatically.
Untracked by version control.

**Instruction**:
Always-on guidance that harnaas writes into the project's committed memory file. Distinct from a rule
in that it survives a fresh clone without anyone running install, and cannot be scoped to particular
paths.

**Command**:
An asset the user invokes deliberately by typing a token for it.

**Persona**:
A delegated worker with its own model and tool budget, which the harness dispatches work to.
_Avoid_: agent, subagent

### The two files

**Manifest**:
`harnaas.json` — the committed, hand-edited declaration of which assets a project wants and where
they come from.
_Avoid_: config, declaration, settings

**Lockfile**:
`harnaas.lock.json` — the machine-written record of what was actually installed and from which
commit. Committed alongside the manifest.
_Avoid_: manifest — note that the entire.io codebase harnaas borrows its architecture from uses
"manifest" for precisely this file and "metadata" for the declaration. harnaas follows npm and Cargo
instead. Do not "correct" this.

### Installing

**Source**:
Where an asset's content comes from — a path within a GitHub repository at some ref, or a path under
the project's `.harnaas` directory.

**Scope**:
Which root an asset installs beneath — `project` for the repository's own harness directory, `user`
for the harness's per-user home.

**Managed**:
Describes a destination recorded in the lockfile. harnaas may update or remove a managed destination,
because it put it there.

**Unmanaged**:
Describes a destination that exists on disk but is not recorded in the lockfile. harnaas never
overwrites or deletes one, on any flag.

**Drift**:
The condition of a managed destination whose content no longer matches what was installed — somebody
edited it outside harnaas.

**Managed block**:
The marker-delimited region of the project's memory file that harnaas owns. Everything outside it is
the team's and is preserved untouched.

### Checking

**Lint**:
The read-only check that the installed state still agrees with the manifest and the lockfile, and
that nothing has moved on upstream. Lint examines the *installation* — never the content of an asset.
_Avoid_: doctor, check, verify

**Finding**:
One problem lint reports, carrying a severity and the command that resolves it.
_Avoid_: issue, error, violation, diagnostic

  the work is gone

options.description: Current spec position: harnaas never edits .gitignore, init just prints a suggestion. Keeps harnaas out of a file teams care about — but having chosen the gitignored model, leaving the ignore rules unmanaged means the model only works if someone maintains them by hand, correctly, forever.

options.label: A .gitignore inside each managed directory
options.description: harnaas owns `.claude/skills/.gitignore` and friends — the convention the entire.io repo already uses for `.claude/`, `.gemini/` and `.entire/`. Keeps the root .gitignore clean, but scatters ownership across several files and still needs per-asset precision inside each one.

questions.question: A fresh CI checkout has the manifest and lockfile but zero installed files. What should `harnaas lint` do there?

options.label: Add a frozen check, plus collapse the noise (Recommended)
options.description: Two separate fixes. A `--frozen` mode verifies the lockfile still satisfies the manifest without needing any files present — the `npm ci` / `cargo --locked` check, and the fast PR gate that catches someone editing harnaas.json without re-running install. Separately, lint collapses 'nothing is installed at all' into one finding rather than N.
options.preview:
PR gate (fast, no network, no install):
  harnaas lint --frozen
  → "lockfile is up to date with manifest"

Full gate:
  harnaas install
  harnaas lint

And if you forget the install step:
  harnaas lint
  → 1 finding: "no assets installed —
     run harnaas install"
     (not 40 separate errors)

options.label: Just collapse the noise
options.description: No new mode. lint detects that nothing is installed and says so once, and the documented CI workflow is always `harnaas install && harnaas lint`. Fewer concepts, but every PR pays for a full network install just to find out the lockfile is stale.

options.label: Put the frozen check on install
options.description: `harnaas install --check` (or `--frozen-lockfile`) rather than a lint flag — matching npm and yarn, where the lockfile-verification mode lives on the install command. Arguably the more familiar placement, but it puts a read-only check on the command that otherwise writes.

options.label: Leave it as specced
options.description: lint reports every declared asset as not-installed, which is literally true. CI is documented to run install first, and that's that. Honest, but a 40-error report for a correctly-configured repo trains people to ignore lint output.

questions.question: Is harnaas.json hand-edited only, or does harnaas get commands that write it?

options.label: Hand-edited only, for v1 (Recommended)
options.description: Sticks to the three commands in your brief. The manifest stays a file humans own, which keeps formatting and comments safe and keeps the manifest spec simple — harnaas only ever reads it. Adding assets means editing JSON by hand, which is a real papercut but a survivable one for a team-scale tool.
options.preview:
$ $EDITOR harnaas.json      # add an entry
$ harnaas install

harnaas reads harnaas.json.
harnaas writes harnaas.lock.json.

Clean split. No formatting-preservation
problem, no JSON round-trip spec.

options.label: Add `add` and `remove`
options.description: `harnaas add github:owner/repo/skills/review@v1` edits the manifest and installs; `harnaas remove code-review` edits it and converges. Much better ergonomics and what anyone coming from npm expects — but harnaas now has to rewrite a hand-formatted file without destroying its layout, which is a spec of its own.
options.preview:
$ harnaas add github:acme/assets/skills/review@v1
  → writes harnaas.json
  → installs
  → writes harnaas.lock.json

$ harnaas remove review
  → removes from harnaas.json
  → deletes files
  → updates lockfile

Cost: harnaas must preserve the user's
formatting when rewriting JSON.

options.label: Add `add` only
options.description: Adding is the frequent, fiddly operation — you have to get the source URI syntax exactly right. Removing is a one-line deletion anyone can do by hand, and convergence already handles the filesystem side. Gets most of the ergonomic win for half the surface.

questions.question: Confirming the word I've written into every spec file and into CONTEXT.md: is `asset` the right umbrella term?

options.label: Yes — `asset` (Recommended)
options.description: Neutral, accommodates 'a directory of markdown' without implying executable code, and collides with nothing: plugin, extension, skill and agent are all already overloaded across this ecosystem, and capability is taken by OpenSpec. Already written throughout the specs and CONTEXT.md.

options.label: `artifact`
options.description: More precise about being a produced, versioned thing — but collides with build artifacts, and with the lockfile's own sense of 'the artifact we recorded'.

options.label: `component`
options.description: Familiar and neutral. Slightly implies composition into a larger whole, which these don't do — each asset stands alone.

options.label: `item`
options.description: Maximally plain and unpretentious. Also nearly contentless — 'the item registry' and 'item resolution' read as though a term were still missing.

content.text: Sixteen decisions settled. Four more — two of these re-examine choices you made earlier, now that the facts have landed.

questions.question: You chose 'registry now, Claude Code first' before I knew that most harnesses have nowhere to put an asset at all. Does that change it?

options.label: Keep the registry (Recommended)
options.description: The cost is one interface, one registry and one boundary test. And the adapter boundary earns its keep for a second reason beyond multi-harness: it isolates destination mapping from install logic, so install is testable without a real .claude tree. The AGENTS.md decision already showed multi-harness thinking paying off — one file, three harnesses.
options.preview:
Types a harness can actually receive:

  claude-code   skill rule instruction
                command persona    (5/5)
  codex         skill persona
                instruction        (3/5)
  gemini        persona
                instruction        (2/5)
  cursor        — nothing          (0/5)
  opencode      — nothing          (0/5)
  copilot-cli   instruction only   (1/5)
  factory       — nothing          (0/5)

Still three real adapters' worth of variation.

options.label: Drop it — hardcode Claude Code
options.description: A registry with one implementation is the textbook premature abstraction, and four of the eight harnesses in that ecosystem can never receive a single asset. Hardcode the paths, extract the interface the day a second adapter actually lands. Costs a refactor later, in exchange for a much smaller v1.
options.preview:
v1: Claude Code paths written inline.

  skill       → .claude/skills/<id>/
  rule        → .claude/rules/<id>.md
  instruction → AGENTS.md block
  command     → .claude/commands/<id>.md
  persona     → .claude/agents/<id>.md

No interface, no registry, no boundary
test, no 'unsupported' outcome state.

Extract when codex actually ships.

options.label: Keep it, but narrow the scope
options.description: Build the registry, and state explicitly that harnaas targets only harnesses with real file-based destinations — Claude Code, Codex, Gemini. Cursor, OpenCode and Factory Droid are documented as permanently out of scope rather than as 'not yet supported', so nobody builds toward them.

questions.question: With installs gitignored, a local `.harnaas/` source is a committed file copied to an ignored location in the same repo. What is that for?

options.label: Keep as specced (Recommended)
options.description: It was in your original brief, and it does two things GitHub sources can't: it's the only way to get a repo-authored asset into ~/.claude at user scope, and it gives locally-authored assets the same drift, lint and convergence handling as remote ones. The project-scope copy is admittedly circular — but uniformity is worth it.
options.preview:
repo/
├── .harnaas/rules/house.md   [committed]
└── .claude/rules/house.md    [ignored]
            ↑ copy of the above

Circular at project scope. But:
• user scope: .harnaas/ → ~/.claude/  ✓
• lint/drift/converge treat local and
  remote assets identically             ✓
• one mental model, not two            ✓

options.label: User scope only
options.description: Local sources are declarable only for assets scoped to the user, where the copy genuinely moves the file somewhere it couldn't otherwise be. At project scope, a team that wants a hand-written skill just commits it to .claude/ directly and doesn't declare it. Removes the circularity, adds a rule to remember.

options.label: Drop local sources in v1
options.description: GitHub sources only. Simplest possible v1 — but it contradicts your original brief, which named local .harnaas paths explicitly, and it leaves no path at all for getting a repo-authored asset into a user-scope harness home.

questions.question: Claude Code rules support a `paths:` frontmatter key that scopes a rule to matching files. Should harnaas do anything with it?

options.label: Pass through, untouched (Recommended)
options.description: harnaas copies content verbatim and never inspects or rewrites frontmatter. If a rule's author wrote `paths:`, it works; if not, the rule is always-on. This is the same principle behind not injecting an ownership marker — byte-equality with the source is what makes drift detection possible, and rewriting frontmatter would destroy it.
options.preview:
source file            installed file
───────────            ──────────────
---                    ---
paths: ["src/**"]  →   paths: ["src/**"]
---                    ---
…content…               …content…

byte-identical → digest comparison works
→ lint can tell drift from an upstream change

options.label: Let the manifest set it
options.description: A manifest entry could carry `paths: ["src/**"]`, and harnaas would write it into the installed rule's frontmatter. Lets a consuming project scope somebody else's rule without forking it — genuinely useful. But now the installed bytes differ from the source bytes, and the whole digest model needs a separate 'expected content' notion.

options.label: Pass through, but validate
options.description: Copy verbatim, and additionally check that a rule asset's `paths` frontmatter parses — failing install with a clear error rather than letting a malformed value silently make the rule never load. Keeps byte-equality, adds a small amount of content awareness that lint is otherwise defined not to have.

questions.question: Where does an `instruction` asset go when it's scoped to the user rather than the project?

options.label: Project scope only (Recommended)
options.description: `instruction` exists as a type distinct from `rule` for exactly one reason: it lives in a committed file and so survives a fresh clone without anyone running install. At user scope there is no clone and no commit, so that property is meaningless and instruction collapses into rule. Declaring one at user scope should be a validation error naming `rule` as the alternative.

options.label: Managed block in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
options.description: Same mechanism, personal file. Consistent — an instruction behaves the same way at both scopes — but it means harnaas edits a file in the user's home that has nothing to do with any project, and the type's defining distinction from `rule` disappears.

options.label: Silently install it as a rule instead
options.description: Accept the declaration and write ~/.claude/rules/<id>.md. Forgiving, and the practical outcome is what the user wanted. But quietly changing an asset's type is exactly the kind of magic that makes a lint report confusing later.

content.text:
Stop — I need to correct something I told you, and it invalidates one of your answers.

**AGENTS.md is not loaded by Claude Code.** The deeper verification found the actual memory loader in the binary (v2.1.227). The path map is exhaustive and hardcoded to `CLAUDE.md` at every scope:

```js
case"User":   return join(En(),"CLAUDE.md");
case"Local":  return join(t,"CLAUDE.local.md");
case"Project":return join(t,"CLAUDE.md");
case"Managed":return join(Kz(),"CLAUDE.md");
```

All 28 `"CLAUDE.md"` literals were enumerated; none has an `AGENTS.md` sibling. The string I relied on — *"Claude Code hardcodes CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md discovery"* — is a **user-facing message with no code behind it** in this build. I quoted it as evidence; it wasn't. AGENTS.md is inert unless something imports it.

`@`-imports **do** work and are verified, so AGENTS.md is still reachable — but only via an import line in `CLAUDE.md`, which makes that line mandatory rather than a nicety. Three more verified facts that change things:

- **Deduplication is real.** Keyed by `realpath`; CLAUDE.md loads before the rules dir, so an imported file wins and the rules walk drops it. No double-injection. **But** an imported rules file bypasses its own `paths:` glob gate and becomes unconditional — a live trap if we ever both import and place the same rule.
- **HTML comments are stripped** before the model sees anything. Marker comments cost zero context — good — but the model cannot distinguish managed from hand-written text.
- **4 MiB hard per-file cap, skipped silently** (debug log only), with a soft warning at ~40,000 chars. The skills cap is 1 MB, not the 64 KB I passed on earlier.

On the registry: you asked for the `openspec init` approach — maximum harness coverage. That reframes it usefully, because `instruction` is the one type nearly *every* harness has, even the four with nowhere to put a skill. I've launched a broad sweep to map that landscape properly rather than guess at it.

content.text: Twenty decisions settled. Updating the glossary — your last answers changed what `instruction` means and introduced a distinction worth naming.

input.old_string:
**Instruction**:
Always-on guidance that harnaas writes into the project's committed memory file. Distinct from a rule
in that it survives a fresh clone without anyone running install, and cannot be scoped to particular
paths.
input.new_string:
**Instruction**:
Always-on guidance that harnaas concatenates into a file it owns outright and the project commits.
Distinct from a rule in that it survives a fresh clone without anyone having run install, and cannot
be scoped to particular paths. Project scope only — at user scope there is no clone, so the
distinction from a rule disappears.

result.output: The file C:\Users\brasp\Documents\GitHub\harnaas\CONTEXT.md has been updated successfully. (file state is current in your context — no need to Read it back)

input.old_string:
**Managed block**:
The marker-delimited region of the project's memory file that harnaas owns. Everything outside it is
the team's and is preserved untouched.
input.new_string:
**Owned file**:
A file whose entire contents harnaas generates, so no part of it is hand-written and drift is a
whole-file comparison.

**Managed block**:
A marker-delimited region harnaas owns inside a file the team also writes. Everything outside it is
preserved untouched. Used where harnaas must contribute to a file it cannot own outright.

**Convergence**:
Install bringing the installed set into agreement with the manifest, including removing assets that
are no longer declared.

questions.question: A team pulling 20 skills from one asset repo would write `github:acme/assets` twenty times with the same ref. Is that acceptable?

options.label: Flat + a shared `sources` block (Recommended)
options.description: Declare each repository and ref once under a top-level key, and have assets reference it. Fixes the sharpest problem — version skew, where you bump the ref in 19 of 20 entries — with the least damage to the model: every installed asset still has exactly one entry and one id, so the lockfile, lint messages and convergence are all unchanged.

options.label: Flat only — repeat the source
options.description: One entry per asset, full source string every time. What the specs say today. Nothing to learn, nothing indirect, and every entry is independently readable — but bumping a shared ref is a find-and-replace, and getting it wrong gives you two versions of the same repo installed at once.
options.preview:
"assets": [
  { "id": "review", "type": "skill",
    "source": "github:acme/assets/skills/review@v1.2.0" },
  { "id": "deploy", "type": "command",
    "source": "github:acme/assets/commands/deploy@v1.2.0" },
  … 18 more, same repo, same ref
]

✓ 每 entry self-contained
✗ version skew is one bad edit away

options.label: Flat + directory expansion
options.description: One entry whose source points at a directory installs every asset under it. Kills the verbosity outright — but the asset id no longer maps to one destination, so lint can no longer say 'asset X drifted' without inventing per-file identity, and you lose the ability to take 5 of the 20.
options.preview:
{ "id": "acme-skills", "type": "skill",
  "source": "github:acme/assets/skills@v1.2.0" }

  → installs review/, refactor/, audit/, …

✓ one entry, one ref, everything
✗ id ≠ destination — breaks lint precision
✗ all-or-nothing; no cherry-picking
✗ upstream adding a skill silently installs it

options.label: All three
options.description: Support flat entries, a shared sources block, and directory expansion. Maximum expressiveness — and three ways to say the same thing, which means three code paths in resolution, three shapes in the lockfile, and a manifest spec that is mostly about its own syntax.

questions.question: lint says v1.3.0 is available. With a hand-edited manifest, how does someone actually take that update?

options.label: lint prints the exact edit (Recommended)
options.description: The finding's remedy is the literal before/after — which file, which line, which string to change — so taking an update is a copy-paste followed by `harnaas install`. Keeps the manifest hand-edited as you chose, while removing essentially all of the friction that decision costs.
options.preview:
$ harnaas lint

  warning  review — newer version available
           harnaas.json:7
           -  "source": "acme:skills/review@v1.2.0"
           +  "source": "acme:skills/review@v1.3.0"
           then: harnaas install

One copy-paste. No new command.
Manifest stays a file humans own.

options.label: Just name the version
options.description: lint reports that a newer tag exists and leaves finding the line to the user. Less output, and the edit is genuinely trivial once you know the version — but with a shared sources block the line to change may not be the one the asset is declared on.

options.label: Add `harnaas update`
options.description: A command that rewrites refs in the manifest to the newest compatible version and installs. Standard package-manager ergonomics and the thing people will reach for — but it directly reverses your hand-edited-only decision, and brings back the JSON formatting-preservation problem you avoided.

questions.question: How should harnaas authenticate to private GitHub repositories?

options.label: Namespaced var, standard fallbacks (Recommended)
options.description: Ref resolution goes over the Git protocol and therefore already works through the user's existing credential helpers — no configuration at all in the common case. For the archive download, read HARNAAS_GITHUB_TOKEN first, then GH_TOKEN, then GITHUB_TOKEN, so a user can scope a token to harnaas without disturbing other tooling.
options.preview:
ref resolution   git credential helpers
                 (already configured, zero setup)

archive download HARNAAS_GITHUB_TOKEN
              →  GH_TOKEN
              →  GITHUB_TOKEN
              →  unauthenticated

Auth failure names the variable it looked for.

options.label: Standard vars only
options.description: GH_TOKEN then GITHUB_TOKEN, with no harnaas-specific variable. One fewer thing to document, and it is what every CI environment already sets — but a user who wants harnaas to use a narrower token than the rest of their tooling has no way to say so.

options.label: Shell out to the `gh` CLI
options.description: Ask `gh auth token` when the CLI is present, falling back to environment variables. Zero-setup for anyone who already uses gh, which is most GitHub users — at the cost of a runtime dependency on an external binary and its auth state.

questions.question: Should `harnaas install` be able to run with no network at all?

options.label: Yes — offline mode over the cache (Recommended)
options.description: Cache lives under the user cache directory, keyed by commit, overridable with HARNAAS_CACHE_DIR. An offline flag resolves every source from the cache alone and fails naming the assets it could not satisfy. Makes installs reproducible in an air-gapped or flaky CI, and costs almost nothing given the cache already exists.

$HARNAAS_CACHE_DIR (or user cache dir)
  archives/<commit>.tar.gz    content-addressed
  refs/<repo>.json            TTL'd resolutions

  ✗ deploy     not cached — needs network

## 3. What the adapter interface must expose

The openspec shape (`{skillsDir, globalSkillsDir}` + one `getFilePath/formatFile` adapter) is insufficient on four axes. Minimum surface:

```ts
type Support = 'native' | 'alias' | 'emulated' | 'unsupported';
type WriteMode = 'own-file' | 'merge-document' | 'marker-block' | 'register-in-config';

interface HarnessAdapter {
  id: string;                        // + alias map, cf. TOOL_ID_ALIASES { windsurf: 'devin' }
  displayName: string;
  detectionPaths: string[];          // straight from openspec; several harnesses need >1

  supports(type: AssetType): Support;

  // per (type, asset, scope) — NOT computable from one root field
  target(type, asset, scope): { path: string; writeMode: WriteMode; root: string }
                            | { unsupported: true; reason: string; via?: AssetType };

  render(type, asset): string;       // per-harness, per-type serializer

  note?(type): string | undefined;   // openspec's setupNote, but keyed by type
  gate?(type): string | undefined;   // "requires Settings > Beta", "requires project trust"
}
```

Why each piece is forced by the data:

- **`target` must be per-(adapter, type), not derived.** openspec's `resolveToolSkillsDir` works because it writes one thing. Cline splits roots: skills in `.cline/skills/`, workflows in `.clinerules/workflows/` — openspec's own table already flags this ("skills and commands land in *different* roots"). Claude namespaces commands by subdirectory (`.claude/commands/opsx/propose.md` → `/opsx:propose`) but not skills. Gemini namespaces with `:` and uses a different extension.
- **`render` per type, not per tool.** Formats that are not markdown-with-frontmatter: Gemini commands (TOML, `prompt` required), Codex personas (TOML), Cline personas (YAML), Warp commands (YAML with `{{arg}}`), Amp personas (TS + magic comment), Cursor rules (`.mdc`, and `.md` there is silently ignored).
- **`writeMode` must be first-class, because four targets are not files harnaas owns.** `merge-document`: Roo `.roomodes` holds every persona in one YAML doc. `register-in-config`: Aider `read:` in `.aider.conf.yml`, Goose `slash_commands:` in `config.yaml`, Kilo/OpenCode `instructions` arrays. `marker-block`: every `instruction` target, all 23. Only skill/rule/persona/command in tool-owned dirs are `own-file`.

**Yes, `unsupported` must be a first-class outcome — 20 of 115 cells (17%) are empty, and that undercounts the problem.** The larger category is *supported-but-differently*: 4 command cells that are actually skills, 5 persona cells with a non-markdown serializer, 5 rule cells that do not glob-scope. A boolean `supports` collapses those into wrong writes. Model it as the four-value `Support` above, with `via?: AssetType` on the unsupported branch so `command → skill` for Codex/Windsurf/Zed/Amp is a routing decision the registry makes, not a special case in the generation loop.

Note that openspec already discovered this need and under-solved it: `resolveCommandSurfaceCapability` returns `'adapter-backed' | 'skills-invocable' | 'none'` — three values — but its `'skills-invocable'` branch is a hardcoded `if (toolId === 'codex')`. With 5 types that hardcode becomes ~13 special cases.

---

## 4. How closely to follow `openspec init`

**Copy directly:**

1. **Two registries joined by id, absence is meaningful** (`dist/core/config.js` `AI_TOOLS` + `dist/core/command-generation/registry.js`). For harnaas this becomes one adapter registry with a sparse 23×5 capability map; the AST import-boundary test is the right enforcement for "no adapter imports another adapter."
2. **`detectionPaths` and the three-signal state model** (detected / configured / fully-configured) driving *presentation only* — pre-selection and `(configured)` / `(detected)` labels — never write behavior. Harnaas needs richer detection paths than openspec: Copilot CLI already needs seven.
3. **`setupNote`**, but keyed per-type. openspec has one (Hermes). harnaas will have a dozen: Trae personas behind Settings > Beta, Windsurf personas behind Subagents (Preview), Codex `.codex/*` inert until project trust, Pi `.pi/prompts` trust-gated, Zed project skills need a trusted worktree, Copilot VS Code `chat.includeReferencedInstructions` defaults false, Cursor user rules are settings-UI-only with no file path.
4. **Per-tool failure collection, aggregate throw at the end** — one broken adapter must not abort the other 22.
5. **`assertPathWithin` / `resolveProjectArtifactPath`** guards. Non-negotiable when tool dirs may be symlinks.
6. **The `generatedBy` frontmatter stamp read back by regex for currency, with byte-comparison as fallback where the format carries no frontmatter.** openspec hit exactly this (`areCommandFilesUpToDate` → `normalizeCommandContent`); harnaas will hit it on Gemini TOML and Warp YAML.
7. **The shared-root ownership marker** (`.agents/skills/.openspec-target`). harnaas needs this an order of magnitude more: openspec's collision is 2 tools on `.agents`; harnaas's is **17 harnesses on `.agents/skills/` and ~12 on `.claude/skills/`**.
8. **Deselect → delete reconciliation driven by the same table** (`removeSkillDirs`, `removeCommandFiles`), and the id alias map (`TOOL_ID_ALIASES { windsurf: 'devin' }`) — needed here for windsurf→devin and roo→zoo.

**Does not transfer:**

1. **"Never write into user files."** This is openspec's central design decision (`dist/core/legacy-cleanup.js` exists only to *un*-write the marker blocks older versions added to `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`) and it works because its one artifact lives in a tool-owned subtree. harnaas's **instruction** type is *defined* as content in a committed memory file the user owns. There is no tool-owned subtree to hide in. harnaas must resurrect what openspec deleted — `OPENSPEC_MARKERS` + `updateFileWithMarkers` with the line-anchored `isMarkerOnOwnLine` check — or use per-harness import syntax where it exists.
2. **Unconditional `FileSystemUtils.writeFile` for everything.** Correct for skill/rule/persona/command in tool-owned dirs; wrong for instruction, wrong for Roo `.roomodes` (shared document), wrong for config-array registration (Aider/Goose/Kilo/OpenCode). openspec already had to invent two exceptions for exactly this — content fingerprinting for Copilot cloud files (`isManagedCopilotCloudFile` / `findUnmanagedCloudFiles`, leaving unrecognized bytes untouched and reporting them) and lossless YAML document editing for `openspec/config.yaml` (`parseDocument` → `doc.setIn` → `doc.toString()`, preserving comments and ordering). **Both of those exceptions become the mainline path for two of harnaas's five types.** Copy the techniques, not the "one write path" architecture.
3. **`resolveToolSkillsDir`'s single `<dir>/skills` formula.** Five types have no common shape; see §3.
4. **One `globalSkillsDir` field.** openspec has exactly one global tool (MiniMax). harnaas's user scope is platform-divergent for several: Warp is `~/.warp/workflows/` (macOS), `%APPDATA%\warp\Warp\data\workflows\` (Windows), `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/warp-terminal/workflows/` (Linux); Goose config is `~/.config/goose/` vs `%APPDATA%\Block\goose\config\`; Windsurf/Devin is `~/.config/devin/` vs `%APPDATA%\devin\`. `path.join(homeDir, tool.globalSkillsDir, 'skills')` cannot express any of these.
5. **The single `if (toolId === 'codex')` fallback.** With five types the fallback graph is real and must be data.

---

## 5. Three highest-risk traps

**Trap 1 — inert by format.** The file lands, the path is right, nothing reads it because the extension or schema is wrong.
- Gemini CLI: `FileCommandLoader` globs `**/*.toml` only. A `.gemini/commands/foo.md` is dead — upstream's own repo carries an inert `strict-development-rules.md` in that directory, and the markdown-commands request (#15535) is **closed as not planned**. TOML also requires a `prompt` key.
- Cursor: "A plain `.md` file in `.cursor/rules` is ignored by the rules system because it has no frontmatter to specify `description`, `globs`, and `alwaysApply`." Must be `.mdc`.
- Warp: `.warp/workflows/*.{yaml,yml}` — a markdown workflow is inert, and the directory only loads inside a git repo.
- Codex: `.codex/agents/<n>.toml`, and a stray `config.toml` in that tree is **rejected by the agent-role scanner at every startup**.
- Roo: `.roo/rules/` silently drops 21 basename patterns including `*.log`, `*.lock`, `*.old`, `*.tmp`.
A naive adapter that emits markdown-with-YAML-frontmatter everywhere gets five of these wrong.

**Trap 2 — inert by removal, with the documentation still live.** Three surfaces in this dataset are *removed*, not deprecated, and each is still described by a published doc page:
- Codex `~/.codex/prompts/<n>.md` — removed in codex-cli 0.117.0; current release is 0.147.0; `learn.chatgpt.com/docs/custom-prompts` is still up. Writing there today is a silent no-op.
- Amp `.agents/commands/` and `~/.config/amp/commands/` — removed Jan 2026; neither string appears in the current manual.
- Windsurf `.windsurf/workflows/*.md` and the whole `~/.codeium/windsurf/` tree — Cascade reached EOL 2026-07-01 and Devin Local does not read workflows, yet the Cascade docs pages carry **no deprecation banner**.
Plus Roo Code entirely (extension discontinued 2026-05-15). Any adapter authored from docs alone produces files nothing will ever read, with no error.

**Trap 3 — inert by identity.** The file is read, parsed, and then dropped because the name is derived from the wrong place.
- **Claude Code contradicts itself between types.** Skills and commands: the *path* names the invocation — `.claude/commands/opsx/apply.md` with `name: "OPSX: Apply"` invokes as `/opsx:apply`; frontmatter `name` is only a display label. Subagents: identity comes *only* from `name:` and "the subdirectory path doesn't affect how a subagent is identified." Same harness, opposite rules, in adjacent directories.
- **`frontmatter.name === parent directory name` is enforced-with-silent-drop** in Augment, Kilo, Cline (mismatch logs a warning and drops the skill), warned in Zed/VS Code, lenient in Pi. Slugging a skill name independently of the directory it lands in loses the skill with no error on three harnesses.
- Roo commands do **no** slugification — `getCommandNameFromFile()` strips only `.md`, so `My Cool Command.md` yields `/My Cool Command`. The lowercase-hyphenate rules apply only to names typed into the settings UI.
- Copilot: "Names with invalid characters cause the skill to silently fail to load," and a `myorg/skill` or `myorg:skill` prefix also silently fails — while plugin-distributed skills get an automatic prefix and must *not* self-prefix.

Runner-up (fold into per-type `setupNote`): **inert by gate.** Files land in the right place with the right name and are still not read — Trae personas need Settings > Beta, Windsurf personas need Subagents (Preview), Codex `.codex/*` and Pi `.pi/*` need project trust, Zed project skills need a trusted worktree, Copilot VS Code needs `chat.useAgentSkills` and `chat.includeReferencedInstructions` (which defaults to **false**).

---

## 6. Open questions — decisions, ranked by consequence

1. **Does harnaas write the `instruction` type into user-owned files at all, and by what mechanism?** Three options: marker block in `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` (openspec's abandoned approach, and the only one that works everywhere); write a harnaas-owned file and inject a one-line import; or refuse and print instructions. The import route works on only ~6 of 23 — Claude Code (`@path`, 4 hops), Gemini (`@path`), Copilot CLI (`@relative`, repo-confined, contested), Amp (`@path` + globs), Windsurf/Devin (`@./path`), Kilo (`{file:...}`). Codex, Cursor's `AGENTS.md`, Pi, Zed, Continue, Augment, Trae, Warp, Factory have **no** import syntax at all. This decision determines whether openspec's core architectural rule survives contact with harnaas's requirements, and it blocks the `WriteMode` enum in §3.

2. **Is `.agents/skills/` the primary write target with per-harness dirs as fallback, or the reverse?** 17 of 23 read it. One write reaches most of the ecosystem — and is simultaneously visible to every installed harness whether the user selected it or not, with per-harness precedence quirks (Gemini: `.agents/` alias *beats* `.gemini/skills`; Cline and Windsurf rank `.agents` below their native dir; Cline's SDK marks `.agents` legacy while its VS Code extension calls it "the opinionated location for new global skills"). Choosing shared-first means a 17-way ownership-marker problem instead of openspec's 2-way one; choosing per-harness means N duplicate skill trees to keep in sync.

3. **When a harness lacks a type: emulate, degrade, or refuse?** Specifically: `command → skill` for Codex/Windsurf/Zed/Amp (4 harnesses, and arguably the right default everywhere given §2); `rule → append to instruction` for the 9 harnesses with no rules directory; `persona → refuse` for Aider/Zed/Warp/Pi (4). This decides whether `target()` returns `Target | Unsupported` or `Target[]`, and whether the CLI's per-harness output can say "3 of 5 written, 2 emulated."

4. **Does v1 ship user-scope targets?** User scope is where the platform divergence lives (Warp's three roots, Goose `%APPDATA%\Block\goose\config\`, Windsurf `%APPDATA%\devin\`, Junie, Copilot JetBrains) **and where precedence inverts** — Claude Code ("enterprise overrides personal, personal overrides project"), Cline ("the global skill takes precedence"), Augment (`~/.augment/skills/` is highest of six). A user-scope write can silently shadow the project-scope write harnaas just made in the same run. Deferring user scope removes ~40% of the path-resolution complexity.

5. **What is the support-tier policy for legacy, removed, and preview surfaces?** Do we emit Claude `.claude/commands/` (legacy but working), Cursor `.cursor/commands/` (works, undocumented, 404s), Copilot VS Code `.github/prompts/` (invisible to Agent Host), Trae/Windsurf personas (preview flags), Roo at all (EOL three months ago)? This decides whether `confidence` is a field that *gates writes* or merely decorates output — and whether the matrix ships three tiers of cell or two.

content.text:
The sweep came back with 23 harnesses adversarially verified, and it moves two things — including one I've now had wrong twice.

**`AGENTS.md` is read natively by 21 of 23 harnesses.** Claude Code is one of only two that don't. So the owned-file-plus-import design we settled on reaches roughly six harnesses, because **import syntax exists in only ~6 of 23** — Codex, Cursor, Pi, Zed, Continue, Augment, Trae, Warp and Factory have none at all. That reverses the reasoning behind your last answer, and I'm putting it back to you rather than quietly patching it.

Three other findings worth having before you answer:

- **`.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is read by 17 of 23.** One write reaches most of the ecosystem.
- **`command` is being absorbed into `skill`.** Seven of the 17 harnesses with a command directory explicitly deprecate it; Codex and Amp *removed* theirs — while the docs pages are still live, so writing there is a silent no-op.
- **`openspec init` tried marker blocks in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and backed out** — it ships a `legacy-cleanup.js` whose only job is un-writing them. That's evidence against the approach, from the exact tool you asked me to follow.

input.old_string:
**Shared target**:
A destination more than one harness reads, so a single write serves several of them. Contrast with a
per-harness target, which only its own harness reads.
input.new_string:
**Shared target**:
A destination more than one harness reads, so a single write serves several of them. Contrast with a
per-harness target, which only its own harness reads.

**Emulated**:
Describes an asset installed through a different type's surface because its own is absent on that
harness — a command delivered as a skill that the model will not invoke on its own. Reported as its
own outcome, never as plain success.

**Support tier**:
How current a harness surface is, which decides whether harnaas will write to it: live surfaces are
written, removed ones are refused, and gated or deprecated ones are written with a note.

questions.question: Emulation breaks an assumption several earlier decisions rest on: that harnaas only ever copies bytes verbatim. It now has to generate some of what it writes.

options.label: Two independent digests — already the shape (Recommended)
options.description: The lockfile already records a source digest and separate per-file installed digests. Rendering just means they legitimately differ. Drift = the installed bytes changed since we wrote them; update = the source bytes changed upstream. Both checks keep working, and 'copy verbatim' becomes the default rendering rather than an invariant.
options.preview:
sourceDigest     what upstream gave us
                 → changed? an UPDATE is available

installedDigest  what harnaas actually wrote
                 → changed? someone EDITED it

copy       installed == source   (common case)
emulate    installed  = render(source)
convert    installed  = toTOML(source)
concat     installed  = join(sources)

No invariant lost. One assumption dropped.

options.label: Copy only — refuse anything needing a transform
options.description: Keep byte-equality as a hard invariant: harnaas installs a file exactly as it found it or not at all. No command emulation, no format conversion for personas, and the instruction marker block would need rethinking since concatenation is already a transform. Simplest possible model — but it reverses the answer you just gave on emulation.

options.label: Render, verify by re-rendering
options.description: Store only the source digest, and at lint time re-run the renderer over the source to compute what should be on disk, comparing that. Nothing derived is stored, so the lockfile stays smaller — but lint now needs the source content in hand, which means it cannot check drift offline or from a cold cache.

questions.question: With `.agents/skills/` reaching 17 harnesses and AGENTS.md reaching 21, 'v1 ships only claude-code' no longer means much. What does v1 actually support?

options.label: Shared targets free, named adapters add depth (Recommended)
options.description: Two tiers. Writing to `.agents/skills/` and AGENTS.md serves skills and instructions for every harness that reads them — no per-harness adapter needed, and harnaas can honestly say so. A named adapter is only required to add that harness's own surfaces: rules, commands, personas. v1 ships one named adapter, Claude Code, and broad shared-target coverage.
options.preview:
shared targets (no adapter needed)
  .agents/skills/   → skill  → 17 harnesses
  AGENTS.md         → instruction → 21

named adapter (v1: claude-code only)
  .claude/rules/    → rule
  .claude/commands/ → command
  .claude/agents/   → persona
  CLAUDE.md         → @AGENTS.md bridge

Adding codex later = one small adapter,
not a new mechanism.

options.label: Named adapters only — claude-code in v1
options.description: A harness is supported only if it has an adapter, full stop. The shared targets are simply where Claude Code's skills happen to land. Honest and narrow — declaring a harness means something concrete — but it undersells what the tool actually achieves and gives no credit for the reach you just bought.

options.label: Ship four named adapters in v1
options.description: claude-code, codex, cursor and copilot — the four with the most complete, adversarially-verified matrices. Much broader real support on day one, at the cost of a substantially larger v1 and four sets of format quirks to get right before anything ships.

questions.question: Should an asset repository declare what it publishes, the way a plugin marketplace does?

options.label: No — the directory convention is the contract (Recommended)
options.description: Inferring type from the containing directory already made the publisher's layout the contract: put a skill in `skills/`, a rule in `rules/`. A separate manifest would restate that, add a second format to spec and version, and create a way for the two to disagree. The consumer names the path; nothing else is needed.

options.label: Optional publisher manifest
options.description: A source repo may ship a file declaring its assets with descriptions and types, which harnaas reads when present and falls back to convention when absent. Enables listing and search later, and lets a publisher use a non-standard layout — but it is a second manifest format to specify, and 'when present' means both paths must be maintained.

options.label: Required for remote sources
options.description: Any repository harnaas installs from must declare its assets. Strongest guarantee that a source is well-formed and intentional about what it publishes — and it makes harnaas unable to install from any repository that has not adopted it, which on day one is every repository.

questions.question: Where can a manifest live — repository root only, or also in subdirectories of a monorepo?

options.label: Repository root only (Recommended)
options.description: One `harnaas.json` and one `harnaas.lock.json` at the root. Harness configuration is repo-wide in practice — `.claude/`, `.agents/` and AGENTS.md all sit at the root — so a per-package manifest would declare assets it cannot install anywhere different. Keeps discovery, locking and convergence single-rooted.
options.preview:
monorepo/
├── harnaas.json         ← the only one
├── harnaas.lock.json
├── AGENTS.md
├── .agents/skills/
└── packages/
    ├── web/
    └── api/

A manifest in packages/web/ would be a
validation error naming the root one.

options.label: Nearest manifest walking up
options.description: Resolve the manifest by walking up from the working directory, so a package inside a monorepo can have its own. Lets teams scope assets per package — but two manifests would then compete to write the same root-level AGENTS.md and `.agents/` directory, and convergence in one could delete the other's files.

options.label: Root plus per-package, merged
options.description: A root manifest establishes shared assets and packages may add their own, merged at install. The most expressive option and genuinely useful in a large monorepo — at the cost of specifying merge semantics, conflict resolution and a lockfile that spans several manifests.

questions.question: The manifest shape you picked showed a `sources` block in its preview, but I never asked about it directly. Confirming it, since I've been assuming it.

options.label: Yes — sources block plus string assets (Recommended)
options.description: Repositories and refs are declared once under `sources`; assets are plain strings referencing them. One ref to bump per repository, and with type and id inferred from the path, most manifests are a short list of strings. This is what the preview you selected showed.

options.label: No block — full source in each asset string
options.description: Skip the indirection: each asset carries its whole source, still as a single string with type and id inferred. Every line is independently readable and there is no key to resolve — but bumping a shared ref means editing every line that uses it, which is the version-skew problem the block exists to remove.
